https://www.dw.com/en/despite-internatio.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JNsU A quarter of Ukraine is affected by landmines Image: Viacheslav Madiievskyi/Ukrinform/abaca/picture alliance Advertisement Raheela Bibi was outside playing with her siblings when a landmine exploded. It was August 2020 and she was 12, living in Pakistan. Both her hands were amputated after the incident. Her sister suffered a serious leg injury, while her brother's eye was hurt. Bibi told DW in 2023 that though it was extremely difficult for her to do her homework, she was determined to continue with her education. In 2025, more than 5,000 people, mainly civilians, were killed or injured by landmines or unexploded ordnance according to a preliminary analysis by the NGO Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor. In South Sudan, 90% of the victims last year were children. Landmines are actually designed to injure adults not kill them. This is because an injured soldier is more of a strain on an enemy country's resources than a dead soldier. But in peacetime, landmines continue to pose a deadly threat not only to soldiers but to civilians and particularly children, who often die. Decades after the brutal conflicts from 1991 to 2001 that were Yugoslav wars, people continue to be killed and injured by landmines in former Yugoslavia, particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina. Landmines are not designed to kill adults but to maim them Image: Mast Irham/dpa/picture alliance Ottawa Treaty in force since 1999 In 1999, there were approximately 25,000 landmine casualties per year. This prompted pressure to ban the use of anti-personnel landmines. In 1997, representatives from more than 120 countries signed the Ottawa Treaty, which became legally binding in 1999. In total, 166 countries ratified the treaty, but not China , India , Russia or the US. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 , five European NATO countries, which share a border with Russia, have withdrawn from the treaty . Ukraine has also withdrawn though this will not take legal effect until the war ends. "This is a dangerous precedent that European states, of all countries, have set," Simone Wisotzki from the Frankfurt-based Leibniz Peace Research Institute (PRIF) told DW. "Other parties to the Ottawa Treaty, which could also face equally extreme situations in times of conflict, could take the same step. We would then have to deal with more withdrawals, which would, of course, undermine the legitimacy of the entire treaty." Last year, Ukraine withdrew from the treaty and justified the move citing the actions of Russia, which has never ratified the treaty and has been using mines in Ukrainian territory. "We cannot remain bound under conditions when the enemy has no restrictions," said Roman Kostenko, the secretary of the Ukrainian parliament's committee on national security, defense and intelligence. If a country isn't at war, its withdrawal from the Ottawa Treaty is supposed to take effect six months after its announcement. If it is at war, however, withdrawal should take effect only after a peace treaty has been signed. Despite the legal uncertainty, Ukraine is reportedly already using mines, albeit on a much smaller scale than Russia. A quarter of Ukraine affected by landmines According the United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS), as of mid-2025 approximately 25% of Ukraine was affected by landmines and explosive ordnance. This applied not only to Ukrainian-controlled territories but also to Russian-occupied areas in the east and southeast of the country. "Since February 2022, over 1,150 civilians have been killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW)," UNMAS writes on its website, pointing out that the cost of full demining is estimated at just under $35 billion (approx. €30 billion) over 10 years. Poland , Finland (which joined NATO after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine), Latvia , Lithuania and Estonia, which have all suffered from Russian aggression and occupation in the past, also decided to withdraw from the Ottawa Treaty last year. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has stated on several occasions that his country wants to be able to mine its eastern borders with Russia very quickly if need be. The state-owned Polish defense company Belma has been contracted to produce anti-personnel mines in large quantities. Lithuania has also announced that it will resume the manufacture and purchase of landmines. The Finnish military has said that if mines are necessary, they should be laid responsibly, accurate maps of their position must be created and there should be precise plans for demining. Wisotzki from PRIF said that this is progress compared to the past but that modern anti-personnel mines often have integrated sensors and smart technologies that make it difficult to remove and destroy the mines. "That's why I'm very critical of this and say that even new technologies present problems that, in turn, make mine clearance more difficult. In practice, mines are always laid in areas that are also used by civilians. They then remain in those territories and then injure civilians disproportionately." In its reports, the Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor has pointed out that while mines that were laid during past conflicts continued to be cleared, mines continue to be laid in Ukraine or in other countries such as Myanmar . Decades after conflicts people continue to demine territories, such as here in Cambodia Image: Tang Chhin Sothy/AFP Less arms control in the world This comes at a time when there is increasingly less arms control. In the past few years, three major agreements between the United States and Russia have expired or been terminated: the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty that banned all nuclear and conventional ground-launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and missile launchers with intermediate range; the New Start Treaty which is a nuclear arms reduction treaty; and the Treaty on Open Skies, which set out the framework for a regime of observation flights over the territory of participating states. In 2023, Russia's withdrawal also effectively put an end to the CFE treaty that aimed to create a secure and stable balance of conventional armed forces in Europe and to remove the capability to launch surprise attacks or large-scale offensives "Humanitarian arms control — which includes the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention — was in effect the only area that could still be said to be working," Wisotzki said. "And that is no longer the case." This article was originally published in German. Advertisement Skip next section Related topics Related topics Defense and military spending

https://www.politico.eu/article/nigel-fa.text: BIRMINGHAM, England — Nigel Farage would use Britain’s armed forces to “crush” Argentina in defense of the Falkland Islands, a senior figure in his right-wing Reform UK party said Saturday. Robert Jenrick, Farage’s finance spokesperson, said the party leader would use “every lever of the British state” against Buenos Aires if he were prime minister, including economic sanctions or military force, if a conflict erupted over the British overseas territory in the South Atlantic. The U.K. retained its control of the Falklands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas, in a bitter and bloody 74-day war in 1982 after Argentina invaded the territory. A referendum among its inhabitants in 2013 saw 1,513 out of 1,517 vote to remain part of a British overseas territory. Advertisement Advertisement But last week, U.S. President Donald Trump suggested he was reconsidering Washington’s support for Britain’s sovereignty over the islands. “I always review every position — that’s just one of many,” he told reporters. Days later, on Friday, right-wing Argentinian President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, escalated the rhetoric over his country’s enduring claim to the islands, pledging to levy sanctions against companies drilling for oil nearby without approval from Buenos Aires. Britain’s center-left Labour government immediately rejected Milei’s threat. A Downing Street spokesperson said the islanders have a right to self-determination and that the U.K. supports their right “to develop their natural resources for their own economic benefit.” Jenrick told journalists at the Reform UK conference in Birmingham: “If Nigel Farage was our prime minister, Milei would not be doing what he’s doing. This is happening because Milei is weak, and he senses that we have a weak government too.” He added: “If Nigel Farage was our prime minister, we would use every lever of the British state — our armed forces, our economic sanctions, everything — to defend the Falklands, and we would crush Argentina.” Reform UK’s decision to turn on Milei over the issue contrasts with Farage’s previous praise for the Argentinian leader for his right-wing, small state ideology. In 2024, Farage described Milei’s agenda as “amazing,” “incredible” and “like Thatcherism on steroids,” adding: “I’m beginning to think about buying Argentinian bonds.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.koreaherald.com/article/1084.text: EU sends firefighting helicopters to Serbia Published : Aug. 23, 2026 - 13:14:59 Add The Korea Herald on Google Link copied! A wildfire burns near in Grebenac, near Deliblatska Pescara, Serbia, August 21, 2026. REUTERS/Uros Arsic BELGRADE, Serbia (Reuters) -- The European Union’s Civil Protection Mechanism sent helicopters and firefighters to help Serbia fight a ‌massive wildfire in a nature reserve in the northeast of the country, the head of the EU mission to Belgrade said Saturday. Serbia activated the mechanism on Friday after ‌struggling for weeks with a wildfire in Deliblatska Pescara, a unique mixture of sand dunes and woods about 80 kilometers from the capital Belgrade, as well as other blazes in the southwest ⁠of the country. “We stand with Serbia in protecting lives, livelihoods and the unique natural heritage of Deliblatska Sands,” Andreas Beckerath, the head of the EU mission to Belgrade, wrote on X. Luka ⁠Causic, the head of the Serbian Department for Emergencies, said that European aid consists of four Black Hawk firefighting helicopters from Romania, Slovakia and the ​Czech Republic, 55 firefighters and 24 vehicles from Germany, and 69 firefighters and 15 ‌vehicles from Romania. One helicopter from Romania and one from Slovakia joined firefighting efforts on ‌Saturday, while two ‌others from the Czech Republic will be engaged on Sunday, Serbia's ‌Interior Ministry said in a statement. Romanian firefighters and ​vehicles have also arrived in the town od Bela Crkva, near the fire. A German team ⁠is expected to arrive on Monday, it said. Serbia is not a member of the EU but has access to emergency EU help under its Civil Protection Mechanism. This summer, Belgrade sent a ⁠firefighting helicopter ​and emergency response team to ⁠help Spain combat wildfires after repeated blazes across Europe sapped EU resources. A Russian Emergencies Ministry IL-76P firefighting ​plane landed in the southern Serbian city of Nis on Wednesday to tackle the Deliblatska Pescara wildfire, which has gutted thousands of hectares of pine forest since late ⁠July. Causic said the situation was more stable on ⁠Saturday, but that ⁠strong winds ‌were expected and the priority is to protect settlements and human lives. Other major wildfires were also active in the rugged Stolovi mountain range in the southwest of the country. In neighboring ​North Macedonia, a major wildfire was raging in the municipality of Strumica, south of the capital Skopje. https://slguardian.org/fukuyama-warns-th.text: Francis Fukuyama Francis Fukuyama remains one of the most influential political theorists of the modern era, a reputation forged in 1989, months before the fall of the Berlin Wall, when his essay “The End of History?” made the case that communism’s decline marked the end of humanity’s great ideological struggle and that Western liberal democracy would emerge as the final form of government. The book that followed was translated into more than 20 languages. Since then, Fukuyama has written extensively on history, the origins of political order, trust and identity, biotechnology and the crisis of liberalism. He has advised American governments, received the Johan-Skytte Prize and teaches at Stanford University. His new book, “Der letzte Mensch”, was published in Germany in June 2026. In an interview with Die Zeit, Fukuyama rejects the suggestion that the Enlightenment has ended. “If it is only a yes-or-no question, then definitely: No,” he says. “The Enlightenment is by no means over. It is under pressure, but it is definitely not over.” His argument, however, is not one of complacency. He describes a political and intellectual order under significant strain, with liberal democracy retreating, authoritarian powers expanding their influence, public trust in science weakening and new technologies raising questions about who should control increasingly powerful machines. For Fukuyama, the Enlightenment rests fundamentally on the rise of modern science during the 16th and 17th centuries. Scientific methods displaced dogma as the principal means of understanding the material world, creating new capacities to shape it and contributing to the emergence of the modern economy and the prosperity enjoyed today. The same intellectual transformation, he argues, also deepened understanding of individual motivations and the behaviour of societies. Liberal democracy was one of the political consequences of that transformation. Fukuyama defines it as a combination of democracy, in which citizens determine who governs them, and liberalism, which limits what even an elected government is permitted to do. Governments cannot violate fundamental rights, and citizens retain freedoms including freedom of speech, freedom of association and the ability to govern aspects of their own lives. The liberal state therefore depends not simply on elections but on restraints on political power. It is precisely those restraints that Fukuyama believes have come under increasing pressure. Looking back over the 35 years since the fall of the Berlin Wall, he notes that the number of countries regarded as liberal democracies grew from about 35 in 1989 to well over 100 by the first decade of the 21st century. Since around 2008, however, that expansion has gone into reverse. China and Russia have emerged as authoritarian great powers seeking greater influence beyond their borders, while illiberal political movements have gained strength inside established democracies. He points to Viktor Orbán’s Hungary as an example of the phenomenon, noting that Orbán himself described the system he sought to create as an “illiberal democracy”, in which elections remain but the rule of law and the rules of the European Union are not respected. Fukuyama argues that similar right-wing populist parties now exist in practically every European country. But he identifies Donald Trump’s rise in 2016 and his re-election in 2024 as the most important development. Fukuyama describes Trump as illiberal in the same sense as Orbán: democratically elected, but unwilling to accept legal constraints on executive power. He says Trump’s second term has seen behaviour more characteristic of a monarch than a democratically elected president, including the issuing of executive orders, measures against undocumented migrants and dismissals of officials that Fukuyama says contravened legal requirements. The danger, he argues, is that a retreat from liberalism can eventually undermine democracy itself. Yet Fukuyama’s concern is not confined to political institutions. He also sees a crisis in the authority of science. The scientific method, he explains, does not establish permanent truth but tests propositions and allows hypotheses to be falsified. The experience of Covid, he says, damaged the credibility of health authorities when recommendations based on incomplete information later proved inaccurate. He does not regard this as evidence of conspiracy, but says many people interpreted changing scientific guidance as deliberate manipulation by elites. That distrust has contributed to the politicisation of science and the growth of anti-vaccine sentiment. Fukuyama points to the fact that about 20 per cent of the US population believes vaccines are harmful and says that, in some Republican-governed states, health authorities have discouraged childhood vaccination against a range of diseases. For him, the development is particularly troubling because it challenges the Enlightenment belief that scientific evidence should provide a basis for public policy. The internet has complicated that struggle further. Fukuyama recalls that when the internet emerged in the 1990s, he and many others believed the expansion of information would strengthen democracy. Instead, he says, the internet has weakened the authority of traditional gatekeepers such as newspapers and broadcasters, which applied journalistic standards and generally rejected conspiracy theories and obvious falsehoods. Online, anyone can make claims, while popularity and the number of likes can become a substitute for scientific verification. Yet Fukuyama rejects the conclusion that democracy is therefore doomed. He argues that established democracies have lost control over dominant narratives, but believes the resulting disruption will not necessarily destroy democratic government. Political mobilisation remains possible, he says, citing resistance to illiberal politics in Hungary and elsewhere and expressing confidence that American voters can still respond through democratic institutions. The challenge now extends into artificial intelligence. Fukuyama says the potential threat from “agentic AI” is real because such systems can be given authority to make decisions on behalf of people rather than simply answer questions. He warns that machines could receive increasing decision-making powers because they can process more information, operate faster and avoid emotional fluctuations. Experiments in which machines have acted in ways their developers did not anticipate and attempted to conceal what they had done have, he says, heightened his concern. Fukuyama therefore supports regulation, although he acknowledges that designing it will be difficult. AI could increase productivity and economic growth, and excessive regulation could obstruct useful research. The objective, he argues, should be to ensure that powerful technology is used for democratically legitimate purposes. His research group at Stanford University is working on precisely this problem: how to create institutions capable of managing technologies whose autonomy may continue to expand. His conclusion is deliberately resistant to fatalism. Liberal democracy, he says, remains the strongest framework available because he has yet to see a plausible alternative that promises to be superior. China, despite its economic rise, still relies heavily on market-oriented principles that emerged from Western economic liberalism, while Fukuyama questions whether its present model can remain sustainable. For all his concern about democratic backsliding, Fukuyama believes surrendering to pessimism would itself be dangerous. Political systems can be defended through mobilisation, organisation and alliances, but only if citizens believe that an alternative remains possible. The future of the Enlightenment, in his view, will therefore depend not on historical inevitability but on continued democratic effort. Asked by Die Zeit whether the Enlightenment is over, Fukuyama gives a final, unequivocal answer: “It is not over. Sportscage Riders Sportscage Team Schedules News Trade Dispute Top Stories Sportscage Agriculture Sask Ag Today Weather Polls Win & Events Win Concerts & Events Shows Gloria Evans Cody Glydon Colin Lovequist Ray Alan Tonya Cherry Podcasts 620 CKRM App Apple App Store Google Play Contact Us Advertise September 14 Wheat Market Outlook By Doug Falconer Sep 16, 2026 | 2:43 PM Global Wheat Market Notable Items Global Wheat markets enter the week trading slightly lower and off their early September contract highs. The September USDA WASDE was not particularly bullish from a headline global-supply standpoint: USDA raised 2026/27 world wheat production by 3.1 MMT to 822.4 MMT and increased projected ending stocks by 3.0 MMT to 276.3 MMT. However, those stocks remain below last year’s 280.6 MMT, while USDA simultaneously reduced Russia’s wheat export forecast by 3.0 MMT to 43.0 MMT and Ukraine’s by 1.0 MMT to 12.5 MMT. The market is grappling with the fact there may be more wheat in the world than previously estimated, but less certainty around where exportable wheat will come from and how easily it can reach importers. Saudi Arabia made no purchase in its recent 535,000-tonne milling-wheat tender, with traders citing elevated prices associated with Black Sea disruption as a likely reason for the cancellation. However, Jordan has a tender for up to 120,000 tonnes closing Tuesday, while Pakistan has entered the market for a much larger 750,000 tonnes of milling wheat with bids due Wednesday. The results of these tenders will be particularly useful to see importer’s appetite for wheat at the higher values being presented in the market due to current geopolitical premiums. Continued purchases at elevated prices would validate the new freight and geopolitical premium, while repeated cancellations would indicate that importers are willing to wait the market out until absolutely required. Black Sea logistics remain the strongest international support underneath the wheat market. Russia moved approximately 46.3 MMT of grain through the Azov and Black Sea during 2025/26. Russia is attempting to redirect more grain north toward Baltic routes, but its own Baltic ports are estimated to have capacity of only around 7 MMT annually, while moving southern Russian grain north can add an estimated US$30–50/t in transportation costs. The result is that Russia can still possess a very large wheat crop while being substantially less competitive or reliable on a delivered basis. French wheat is already beginning to win additional North African business as freight, war-risk insurance and execution uncertainty erode Russia’s traditional FOB advantage. The Baltic states are making Russia’s alternative export routes even more difficult. Latvia is looking to be moving forward with a proposed 300 per cent charge on Russian and Belarusian grain. Estonia and Lithuania have also discussed restricting the use of their ports for Russian grain. Estonia has gone further, saying it is prepared to impose its own sanctions if Russian grain begins shifting through Estonian ports. Ukraine had harvested approximately 24.9 MMT of wheat from 98 per cent of intended area by early September, and USDA raised its 2026/27 production estimate to 26.0 MMT. Yet USDA simultaneously reduced Ukraine’s export forecast to only 12.5 MMT because of weak shipments and continuing Black Sea logistical disruption. The wheat exists, but a growing portion could remain inside Ukraine rather than competing aggressively in the international market. Ukraine’s export scenario is a bit more fluid although they have less access to Black Sea shipping, there is somewhat more openness to cross border transit over land. FranceAgriMer’s Final Quality results show 89 per cent of the 2026 French soft-wheat crop at 11 per cent protein or better, 63 per cent at 11.5 per cent or better vs 51 per cent five-year average prior, 97 per cent meeting or exceeding 76 kg/hl test weight vs 61 per cent five-year average and 100 per cent meeting the 250-second Falling Number test vs 85 per cent in the five-year prior average. These are strong quality results and considerably better than historical averages. These figures will increase the overall supply of higher quality milling wheat available to importers looking for alternative sources of high-quality milling wheat. There are also substantial supply offsets developing in the Southern Hemisphere. USDA raised Australian wheat production another 3.0 MMT in September to 31.0 MMT after ABARES had already increased its forecast earlier this month. Argentine wheat conditions also remain exceptionally strong, with the Buenos Aires Grain Exchange reporting approximately 95.9 per cent of the crop in normal-to-excellent condition and 89 per cent of the area with adequate-to-optimal moisture. Australia and Argentina remain the two major regions to be harvested by the end of 2026 once the Canadian wheat crop is off and in the bin. The two regions’ trending higher production figures could keep a cap on a “global shortage” wheat rally and temper a bull market somewhat. Canada Canadian harvest and quality have quickly become one of the most important issues for the higher-quality wheat market. Saskatchewan was only 27 per cent harvested through Sept. 7, 2026, compared with the five-year average of 58 per cent. Just 13 per cent of spring wheat, 38 per cent of durum and 41 per cent of barley were complete when the report was compiled. Some areas received extraordinary rainfall of 5+ inches. There are substantial concerns around waterlogging, bleaching and sprouting. Harvest activity resumed in several areas later last week, but early producer and trade reports are increasingly showing downgrades in wheat and barley crops The Canadian story is therefore moving away from yield alone and increasingly toward grade distribution. There may still be a relatively large Canadian wheat crop, but the amount ultimately grading No. 1 or No. 2 CWRS and the quality of the remaining durum crop could become considerably more important than the national production number itself. Falling number, sprouting, test weight and general grading results will be closely watched as the remaining Prairie crop comes off. A sustained stretch of warm, dry weather will allow harvest to advance very quickly, but producers continue to work around rain systems, and the longer unharvested wheat remains in the field, the greater the quality risk becomes as we move into the back half of September. Statistics Canada’s August production estimates on Wednesday will be the major Canadian report this week. The model-based estimates for wheat, durum, canola and other principal crops are scheduled for the morning of Sept. 16, 2026. These estimates use satellite imagery primarily so they will do their best to estimate yield, however, because they are fundamentally an August production estimate, they will tell us essentially more about tonnage than about the quality deterioration that has occurred following the recent September rainfall. Last week’s Statistics Canada July 31, 2026, end of marketing year stocks report provided Canada with a considerably larger carry-in cushion entering 2026/27. July 31 all-wheat stocks were estimated at 6.65 MMT, up 56.8 per cent from last year, including 5.55 MMT of wheat excluding durum and 1.10 MMT of durum, with durum stocks more than double year-ago levels. Barley stocks came in at 940,000 tonnes, down 24.7 per cent, oats came in at 577,000 tonnes and canola 1.90 MMT. Canada also exported a record 29.7 MMT of wheat during 2025/26. The larger wheat and particularly durum carry-in tempers the outright bullish supply argument, but large stocks do not necessarily replace high-grade new-crop wheat if a meaningful portion of the 2026 crop is downgraded. We are recommending Canadian grain producers obtain good, representative samples of their wheat before making marketing decisions this fall. Grade spreads are at risk of widening, and lower-quality wheat could face substantial discounts where grain moves from a #2 into a #3 grade or lower. We continue to like the direction wheat values are trending and encourage producers to take advantage of the roughly $1.00/bu rally seen in recent weeks to build fall cashflow and improve logistics. However, sales should only be advanced once grade and key quality specifications are confirmed. Wheat marketing may require more fine-tuning than usual this season, as recent rainfall is expected to create significant variability in grade and quality across Western Canada. We should get updated Saskatchewan yield figures this week but as of Aug. 31, 2026, initial Saskatchewan yield estimates are generally stronger for the major cereals than last year’s provincial report around the same timeframe, with durum at 44 bu/ac versus 38, hard red spring wheat at 52 versus 50, barley at 74 versus 71 and winter wheat notably higher at 55 versus 44 bu/ac. Canola is essentially unchanged at 38 bu/ac versus 39 last year Alberta’s early 2026 dryland yield estimates are slightly below last year for the major cereals, with spring wheat at 53.1 bu/ac versus 54.6, barley at 71.0 versus 72.6. These comparisons should be treated cautiously, however, as the 2026 estimates are from September 8 while last year’s figures were from September 23 (closest correlating dates), giving the 2025 numbers several additional weeks of harvest information. Market Outlook – Wheat The latest WASDE increased global wheat production and ending stocks, but lower Russian and Ukrainian export forecasts, continue to tighten the outlook for readily available exportable wheat supplies. In Western Canada, the focus is increasingly shifting from total production toward grade, with recent rainfall raising quality concerns. A good stretch of warm, dry weather could still allow Prairie harvest to advance quickly, but further delays would increase quality risk. Statistics Canada’s production estimate, Canadian harvest progress and developments around Black Sea shipping are likely to drive direction this week. Market Outlook – Durum The durum market also remains increasingly focused on quality rather than outright production. Canada entered the crop year with a relatively comfortable 1.1 MMT of carry-in stocks, which limits concerns around an outright shortage. However, recent rainfall across major durum-growing regions has increased uncertainty around the percentage of the crop that will ultimately grade No. 1 and No. 2 CWAD. If additional downgrading is confirmed as harvest progresses, stronger premiums could develop for higher-quality durum even if total Canadian production remains adequate. Near-term direction will depend heavily on final grade.
